candidates.text:
If you use frontier models (Opus, Sol, Fable, Astra) and know how to use agentic harnesses effectively, you’re already ahead

I’ve been living in Europe for the last 3 years and 
∙ most my friends are absolutely not vibe coding or care to 
∙ they default to ChatGPT and use it for search or image gen 
∙ Revolut Ultra which is one of EU’s biggest fintechs gives you free ChatGPT Go sub, which caps you at Luna
∙ AI subs cost more in Europe, because you have VAT + it’s priced differently in euros
∙ most my friends have never heard of Grok Bot or Hermes
∙ some have recently heard about Muse (power of Meta’s distribution) 
∙ I onboarded some to instinct or tab and they’re shocked 

Last month in China was interesting for me too. ChatGPT and Claude are both blocked in Hong Kong and Mainland. It’s also illegal to use VPNs in Mainland but I met some people who were accessing western AI because they mentioned reasoning is better + there is better context on the west. 

Conversely, I personally found using Deepseek, Dots (rednote’s model), Ant ling’s models, and Wendao’s models best for information while traveling

It’s interesting to observe and think about all of this because frontier models ARE trained on the entire web yet context + token windows and how partitioned geographies can be with what data is available (most of Chinese web is behind superapps and not accessed like a website) mean what we get limited. It’s also why creative output on AI, even frontier models is absolute crap without references and multiple iterations 

TLDR if you see this post you’re in a bubble, most of the planet hasn’t caught up yet, and AI usage varies greatly across the world

candidates.text:
Big companies have scale. Small companies have speed. I wonder how much AI changes that trade-off.

In a tiny startup, a weekly update feels absurd. You've just spent countless hours working alongside the people you'd be updating. They know.

As companies grow, keeping everyone in sync becomes part of the job. You need meetings, updates, reports etc. and decisions travel through layers of people. That's the price of being big. Coordination at scale is slow and expensive.

That could change with AI. It could cut a lot of that cost - by sharing context, spotting dependencies and helping teams make decisions without so much back and forth.

Now imagine a big company that keeps its distribution, capital and brand but gets back some of a startup's speed.

AI will make small teams more powerful. But the big companies that adopt it well could end up moving much faster than they ever have.

Suddenly your competitor is thinking: "Holy shit, they're big AND fast."

We generated 100M+ Instagram views without posting on our main brand account. 

At @kulfiapp, we run 15–20 Instagram pages, each with its own character, audience, and content style. 

Here's how I think about distribution.  

If we run one account, we're relying on that single page to consistently perform.  

With 20 accounts, we're increasing the surface area for virality. Any video from any account could take off.  

we don't need every account to go viral. I just need one video from one of these accounts to take off every couple of days. 

Our strongest growth months happened while our official Instagram account was completely inactive.

We've essentially increased the probability of going viral by giving ourselves more chances to make it happen.

candidates.text:
.@dawallach explains why the success of GLP-1s, which took decades to develop inside big pharma rather than a startup, shows just how difficult it is to turn drug ideas into treatments, even with AI:

 D.A.: "The bottleneck is not ideas... The challenge right now, even before AI, was that we have a superabundance of good ideas for new drugs. You can go look at any university in America or now in China and Europe. Great science everywhere."

John: "Every time a new blockbuster drug comes out, I do the research on where it came from and it's like a guy invented it in the '80s and then it was used for some really small thing in the '90s, and then they finally got it to scale in the 2010s."

D.A.: "The GLPs are one of those stories. It's kind of an indictment of the startup ecosystem. That didn't come from a startup. The story in big pharma has been all the new drugs come from M&A.

But the GLPs are the biggest, and they didn't. They were like a 20-year project inside of big pharma.

AI, from the standpoint of a big pharma company, is going to chip away in incremental ways at a million different things... Maybe a drug's development time goes from 12 years to 11 years and then maybe to 10 years... But is it going to cure cancer overnight? Is it going to solve aging overnight? Those are sales pitches."
